tests.title: Data Structures Test: BST & Tree Balancing
tests.subject: Data Structures
tests.question: Explain search operations in an unbalanced BST vs an AVL tree.
tests.model_answer: In an unbalanced BST, search complexity is O(h) which degenerates to O(n) in worst case (skewed tree). In an AVL tree, self-balancing guarantees height is O(log n), so search is always O(log n).
tests.rubric: Unbalanced BST complexity: 5 marks; AVL self-balancing & O(log n) search: 5 marks

tests.title: Machine Learning Test 1: Supervised Learning & Optimization
tests.subject: Machine Learning & AI
tests.question:
1. Explain the fundamental concept of Gradient Descent in Supervised Learning.
2. Differentiate between Batch Gradient Descent and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD).
3. Why is the learning rate hyperparameter crucial?
tests.model_answer:
1. Gradient Descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize the cost/loss function by moving in the direction of steepest descent (negative gradient of the loss with respect to parameters).
2. Batch Gradient Descent computes gradients over the entire dataset before updating parameters (stable but slow on large datasets). SGD updates weights for each individual training example (fast, introduces noise that helps escape local minima).
3. The learning rate controls the step size taken during each iteration. A very high learning rate can overshoot the global minimum and diverge; a very small learning rate leads to extremely slow convergence.
tests.rubric: Cost function minimization: 3 marks; Batch vs SGD distinction: 4 marks; Learning rate explanation & tradeoffs: 3 marks.

AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments
1. Abstract
Manually grading handwritten assignments is slow and inconsistent: a teacher with a large class may
spend eight to ten hours reading, interpreting handwriting, judging correctness, and writing
feedback for a single assignment. This document presents the research and design for an AI-
powered assignment evaluation platform that automates this workflow end to end. The system
accepts a photograph of a handwritten answer, cleans it using classical computer vision techniques,
converts the handwriting to machine-readable text using deep-learning-based Optical Character
Recognition (OCR), and then uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to semantically compare the
student's answer against a model answer, producing marks and constructive feedback within
seconds. The complete platform is built on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, Node.js)
and exposes separate dashboards for teachers and students.
2. Introduction and Problem Statement
In a typical classroom of about 100 students, a teacher must read every submitted answer sheet,
decipher individual handwriting styles, judge whether the answer is conceptually correct, assign
marks, and write feedback for each student. This process is repetitive, time-consuming, and prone to
inconsistency between different graders or even the same grader across a long session.
The goal of this project is to replace this manual process with an AI Tutor that can perform the same
evaluation automatically: a student uploads a photograph of their handwritten answer, and within
seconds the system returns marks and detailed feedback. This reduces teacher workload
significantly while giving students faster, more consistent feedback on their work.
3. Objectives
● Automate the evaluation of handwritten assignments from image capture to final feedback.
● Apply classical computer vision techniques to clean noisy, tilted, or poorly lit handwritten
images before recognition.
● Use a deep-learning OCR model to accurately convert handwriting into digital text.
● Use a Large Language Model to semantically evaluate the extracted answer against a
teacher-provided model answer, rather than relying on rigid keyword matching.
● Generate marks and human-readable feedback automatically and store them for later
review.
● Provide separate, role-based dashboards for teachers and students built on the MERN stack.
4. Proposed System Overview
The system follows a linear pipeline: a student uploads an image of their handwritten answer, which
is progressively cleaned, digitised, evaluated, and stored before being surfaced back to both the
student and the teacher through their respective dashboards.

5. Module 1 — Image Preprocessing with OpenCV
A photograph taken by a student's phone is rarely clean: it may suffer from poor lighting, shadows,
tilt, blur, or background noise. OCR accuracy depends heavily on image quality, so the first stage of
the pipeline uses OpenCV — a computer vision library, not a machine learning model — to prepare
the image.
5.1 Preprocessing Steps
● Grayscale conversion — OCR performs better on grayscale images than on raw colour
images.
● Noise removal — eliminates small artefacts (specks, dust, stray marks) that could be misread
as characters.
● Thresholding (binarisation) — converts the image into pure black text on a white
background, sharpening the boundary between ink and paper.
● Deskewing — straightens a photo taken at an angle so text lines are horizontal.
● Cropping — removes irrelevant background such as the desk, hands, or other objects,
isolating just the answer sheet.
● Line segmentation — separates the answer into individual lines to make downstream OCR
more reliable.
It is worth clarifying that OpenCV itself is not machine learning; it applies classical image-processing
algorithms such as edge detection, filtering, thresholding, and contour detection.
6. Module 2 — Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
Once the image is cleaned, OCR converts the handwritten content into machine-readable text.
Unlike OpenCV, modern OCR engines are themselves deep-learning models, trained on large
datasets of handwritten samples, and therefore qualify as AI.
6.1 Comparison of OCR Options

For a college-level project, PaddleOCR offers the best balance of accuracy, speed, and ease of
integration. TrOCR can additionally be benchmarked against PaddleOCR to demonstrate a deeper
comparative evaluation of OCR approaches within the project report.
3
AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments
7. Module 3 — Answer Evaluation with a Large Language Model
The OCR stage produces raw text, but the system still needs to judge whether that text represents a
correct answer. This is the role of the LLM (for example GPT, Llama, Gemma, or Mistral). The teacher
first supplies a model answer or rubric — for instance, for the question "Explain Photosynthesis," the
key points might be that it uses sunlight, uses chlorophyll, produces glucose, and produces oxygen.
The LLM then compares the student's extracted answer against this model answer, checking
relevance, presence of key concepts, missing points, and overall correctness of explanation.
Crucially, this comparison is semantic rather than a simple keyword match: a phrase like "plants
make food using sunlight" and "sunlight helps plants produce glucose" express closely related ideas
even though the wording differs, and the LLM is able to recognise this equivalence.
7.1 Example Output
Field Example Value
Marks 7 / 10

Good answer overall — mention chlorophyll and oxygen production, and explain
Feedback
how glucose is formed
8. Module 4 — Data Storage (MongoDB)
Every evaluation — the student's identity, the question, the assigned marks, the generated
feedback, and the submission date — is persisted in MongoDB so that it can be retrieved later by
both students and teachers, and so that class-level performance can be tracked over time.
9. Module 5 — Teacher and Student Dashboards
9.1 Teacher Dashboard
● Create assignments and add questions
● Upload model answers or rubrics
● View student submissions
● Review AI-generated marks and feedback, and override them where necessary
● Track class performance over time
9.2 Student Dashboard
● Upload assignment photographs
● View marks and feedback
● Review previous submissions
● Track personal improvement over time
4
AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments
10. Where Is Machine Learning Actually Used?
Not every stage of the pipeline is AI-driven; it is useful to be explicit about this distinction, both for
architectural clarity and for the project viva.
Pipeline Stage Technology Is it AI?
Image cleaning OpenCV No — classical computer vision
Handwriting recognition (OCR) PaddleOCR / TrOCR Yes — deep learning
Answer evaluation GPT / Llama / Gemma Yes — deep learning (Transformers)
Plagiarism detection (optional
Embeddings Yes — machine learning
extension)
Diagram checking (optional
CNN Yes — deep learning
extension)
11. Recommended Technology Stack
Layer Technology
Frontend React.js with Tailwind CSS or Bootstrap
Backend Node.js with Express.js
Database MongoDB
File storage Cloudinary or AWS S3
Image preprocessing OpenCV
OCR PaddleOCR (primary), optionally benchmarked against TrOCR
Answer evaluation GPT / Llama / Gemma / Mistral (LLM API)
12. Significance of the Project
This project goes beyond a standard CRUD web application by combining several modern technology
layers into a single, coherent system: the MERN stack for the web application itself, OpenCV for
image preprocessing, deep-learning OCR for handwriting recognition, and an LLM for semantic
answer evaluation and feedback generation, with MongoDB and cloud storage handling persistence.
Rather than simply digitising the submission process, the system addresses a genuine, recurring
problem — the time cost of manual grading — while giving students faster and more consistent
feedback.
13. Conclusion
The AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments demonstrates how classical computer vision, deep-
learning OCR, and Large Language Models can be combined within a conventional MERN web
application to automate a task that is traditionally slow and manual. The proposed architecture is
modular — image preprocessing, OCR, and LLM evaluation are each independent stages — which
makes the system straightforward to build incrementally, test stage by stage, and extend later with
5
AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments
optional features such as plagiarism detection or diagram checking. This makes it a strong candidate
for a Software Group Project, since it offers clear scope for individual module ownership, measurable
milestones, and a demonstrable end-to-end system by completion.
14. References
● OpenCV documentation — opencv.org
● PaddleOCR — PaddlePaddle handwriting/text recognition toolkit
● TrOCR: Transformer-based Optical Character Recognition, Microsoft Research
● Google Cloud Vision API documentation
● MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, Node.js official documentation (MERN stack)

even though the wording differs, and the LLM is able to recognise this equivalence.

AI Tutor for Handwritten Assignments
1. Abstract
Manually grading handwritten assignments is slow and inconsistent: a teacher with a large class may
spend eight to ten hours reading, interpreting handwriting, judging correctness, and writing
feedback for a single assignment. This document presents the research and design for an AI-
powered assignment evaluation platform that automates this workflow end to end. The system
accepts a photograph of a handwritten answer, cleans it using classical computer vision techniques,
converts the handwriting to machine-readable text using deep-learning-based Optical Character
Recognition (OCR), and then uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to semantically compare the
student's answer against a model answer, producing marks and constructive feedback within
seconds. The complete platform is built on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, Node.js)
and exposes separate dashboards for teachers and students.
2. Introduction and Problem Statement
In a typical classroom of about 100 students, a teacher must read every submitted answer sheet,
decipher individual handwriting styles, judge whether the answer is conceptually correct, assign
marks, and write feedback for each student. This process is repetitive, time-consuming, and prone to
inconsistency between different graders or even the same grader across a long session.
The goal of this project is to replace this manual process with an AI Tutor that can perform the same
evaluation automatically: a student uploads a photograph of their handwritten answer, and within
seconds the system returns marks and detailed feedback. This reduces teacher workload
significantly while giving students faster, more consistent feedback on their work.
3. Objectives
● Automate the evaluation of handwritten assignments from image capture to final feedback.
● Apply classical computer vision techniques to clean noisy, tilted, or poorly lit handwritten
images before recognition.
● Use a deep-learning OCR model to accurately convert handwriting into digital text.
● Use a Large Language Model to semantically evaluate the extracted answer against a
teacher-provided model answer, rather than relying on rigid keyword matching.
● Generate marks and human-readable feedback automatically and store them for later
review.
● Provide separate, role-based dashboards for teachers and students built on the MERN stack.
4. Proposed System Overview
The system follows a linear pipeline: a student uploads an image of their handwritten answer, which
is progressively cleaned, digitised, evaluated, and stored before being surfaced back to both the
student and the teacher through their respective dashboards.

5. Module 1 — Image Preprocessing with OpenCV
A photograph taken by a student's phone is rarely clean: it may suffer from poor lighting, shadows,
tilt, blur, or background noise. OCR accuracy depends heavily on image quality, so the first stage of
the pipeline uses OpenCV — a computer vision library, not a machine learning model — to prepare
the image.
5.1 Preprocessing Steps
● Grayscale conversion — OCR performs better on grayscale images than on raw colour
images.
● Noise removal — eliminates small artefacts (specks, dust, stray marks) that could be misread
as characters.
● Thresholding (binarisation) — converts the image into pure black text on a white
background, sharpening the boundary between ink and paper.
● Deskewing — straightens a photo taken at an angle so text lines are horizontal.
● Cropping — removes irrelevant background such as the desk, hands, or other objects,
isolating just the answer sheet.
● Line segmentation — separates the answer into individual lines to make downstream OCR
more reliable.
It is worth clarifying that OpenCV itself is not machine learning; it applies classical image-processing
algorithms such as edge detection, filtering, thresholding, and contour detection.
6. Module 2 — Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
Once the image is cleaned, OCR converts the handwritten content into machine-readable text.
Unlike OpenCV, modern OCR engines are themselves deep-learning models, trained on large
datasets of handwritten samples, and therefore qualify as AI.
